title: Ninety Days on the Old Road

setup.context: In my sixties I did something some people thought was foolish. Let me tell you about the motorcycle, and about my old teacher.

paragraphs.text: I had an old motorcycle, a machine from the eighties that my cousin kept running for thirty years. The engine sounded like an argument. One spring I decided to ride it from the coast to the hills, on the old roads my father used to talk about.
Bhaskar-ji, who was nearly eighty by then, told me it was too much for a man my age. You are not a young man anymore, he said, and then he gave me a list of the best tea stalls along the way.

Ninety days. Small towns, dusty crossroads, bridges with no railings. I met farmers whose fields had thinned out, shopkeepers who had moved to the city and come back, schoolchildren who asked whether I was a film star.
The body complained every single day. The back, the knees, the hands on the handlebars. But every evening there was a conversation worth the discomfort, and every morning there was another road.
I came home thinner and quieter, with a notebook of names I had promised to write to. I have kept most of those promises.

reflection.insight: Sometimes you have to leave the familiar road to remember what you were looking for. The discomfort is part of the lesson, not an obstacle to it.
reflection.question: What road have you been meaning to take for years?

follow_up_options: Weren't you scared on those roads?
What did Bhaskar-ji say when you got back?

responses_to_follow_ups.bike: It broke down twice, and my cousin drove out both times with a toolbox and a lot of opinions. It got me home.
responses_to_follow_ups.scared: Often, especially on the bridges. Fear is useful on a motorcycle. It keeps you honest about your speed.
responses_to_follow_ups.back: He asked me how many tea stalls I had visited, and whether I had told the farmers the truth about the rain. Then he told me to go to sleep.
